**Torturer:** You hear that hum?

**Captive:** …What is it?

**Torturer:** The generator. Old machine. Very honest. When it starts, it doesn’t stop halfway out of pity.

**Captive:** I don’t know any password.

**Torturer:** You do. You’ve said it silently three times since you sat down. People always rehearse what they’re afraid to lose.

**Captive:** You’re guessing.

**Torturer:** I don’t guess. I narrow.  
(leans closer)  
Your company rotates credentials every quarter. You hate change. You reused your daughter’s birth month in two old logins. You think no one notices patterns because patterns feel private.

**Captive:** Leave my family out of this.

**Torturer:** Then keep them out of this. Give me the password, and they remain a word you said, not a file I open.

**Captive:** You’re bluffing.

**Torturer:** Am I?  
(taps a metal instrument against the table; a sharp ring)  
Listen carefully. That sound is ten minutes away from your hand.

**Captive:** You can’t do this.

**Torturer:** I already am. This room is the “doing.” Pain is just the punctuation mark at the end of your sentence. You decide when I place it.

**Captive:** I want a lawyer.

**Torturer:** You want delay. Delay is expensive.  
(checks watch)  
Nine minutes.

**Captive:** I told you, I don’t—

**Torturer:** Don’t lie in fragments. It insults both of us.  
(softly)  
Try this instead: start with the first character.

**Captive:** …

**Torturer:** Silence feels powerful right up until it costs you something you can’t replace.

**Captive:** If I tell you, you’ll still hurt me.

**Torturer:** Maybe. Maybe not. But if you don’t tell me, there is no “maybe.” There is only sequence. Finger. Wrist. Elbow. You can count as we go if numbers comfort you.

**Captive:** You’re sick.

**Torturer:** No. I’m focused.  
(slides a photo across the table)  
You were focused once too. This is your office desk, taken yesterday. Coffee stain shaped like a comma. Sticky note under the monitor. You always hide reminders in plain sight.

**Captive:** Give me that.

**Torturer:** Password.

**Captive:** …

**Torturer:** Eight minutes.

**Captive:** Stop counting.

**Torturer:** Then stop earning numbers.

**Captive:** You think pain makes people honest?

**Torturer:** No. Fear of pain makes people practical. Honesty is irrelevant. I only need accuracy.

**Captive:** And if I give you a fake one?

**Torturer:** Then the machine tells me before your scream does.  
(pauses)  
I admire your will. Truly. But will is a candle in wind. I am offering you a door before the storm takes it.

**Captive:** …You won’t touch them?

**Torturer:** Give me the password, and this room gets smaller. Refuse, and your world does.

**Captive:** It’s—  
(stops, swallows)  
If I say it, you let me breathe for a minute.

**Torturer:** You have thirty seconds. Start with the first character.

**Captive:** Capital R.

**Torturer:** Good. See? We can still be civil.

**Captive:** Then a seven. Then…  
(voice shakes)  
Then “aster.”

**Torturer:** “R7aster”… Continue.

**Captive:** Hyphen. “June.” No, wait—  
(closes eyes)  
No. No, don’t turn that on. I’ll give it to you. I’ll give you all of it.

**Torturer:** I know. That’s why the machine is still only humming.

A doorknob.

It turns.

And from the darkness on the other side, someone grabs her wrist.

Rain worked the fire escape like bony fingers on a cheap piano, and the city played along—off-key, half-drunk, and mean.

I sat in the dark with my case open on the table, tools of the trade laid out like sins at confession. Metal and glass. Precision and consequence. Every piece with one job, every job with one ending. My hands moved out of habit, and habit is just guilt that learned choreography.

People think men like me are born without a conscience. That’d be easier. Truth is, conscience is always there—it just talks softer than hunger, and bills, and the kind of promises desperate men make in back rooms with no windows.

I told myself the old lies while I worked.  
*He’s a bad man.*  
*The world breathes easier without him.*  
*If not me, someone else.*  
Lies polished smooth from years of use, fitting the mind like a well-worn glove.

The parts came together in silence, each click sounding louder than thunder in my head. I checked everything twice, then a third time, not because I doubted the gear—because I doubted the man holding it. A mistake in my line of work isn’t a typo. It’s a widow. It’s a headline. It’s a ghost that learns your first name.

Somewhere across town, a man was laughing into a glass he didn’t earn, under lights he thought made him untouchable. Somewhere else, someone was praying he wouldn’t see tomorrow.

And me? I was stuck in the middle, where men like me always end up—between justice and murder, pretending there’s daylight between the two.

The city clock coughed up another minute. Time to move.

I closed the case and killed the lamp. In the dark, my reflection disappeared from the window, and for a second I wondered if that was mercy—or just practice.

Rain had been falling since dusk, not hard, just steady enough to turn the alley into a narrow trench of black water and reflected neon. It ran off rusted fire escapes and cracked gutters, drummed against dented trash lids, and soaked cardboard boxes until they sagged and collapsed like old lungs.

Detective Mara Kline stepped under the yellow wash of a portable floodlight and stopped just short of the chalk markers.

The body lay half on its side, half on its back, one arm bent under the torso at a wrong angle. The victim’s coat had been cut open from sternum to navel, the fabric peeled away and pasted to the wet concrete with blood. Not fresh—most of it had already gone dark, thickening around the seams like spilled motor oil. Rainwater diluted the outer edges into pink threads that ran downhill toward the storm drain.

A patrol officer gagged softly behind his mask. Kline didn’t look up.

“Time found?” she asked.

“Twenty-two nineteen,” said CSU tech Ramirez, crouched by the victim’s boots with a camera. “Call came from a cook taking smoke break in the diner on Seventh.”

Kline nodded once. She pulled on a second pair of nitrile gloves over the first, then knelt. The cold bled through her slacks immediately. She leaned close without touching, eyes tracking details the way a surgeon tracks vessels.

Three deep punctures under the left clavicle, close and deliberate. Not a frenzied attack—clustered, efficient. Defensive wounds on the right hand: split knuckles, torn skin over the index finger, one nail ripped down to the quick. Bruising along the jawline suggested the first hit had been blunt and hard. He’d gone down before the cutting started.

The air smelled of wet brick, fryer grease drifting from the diner vent, and the copper bite of blood that even rain couldn’t wash away. Under that sat another odor, sweet and sickly—intestinal rupture, maybe, or stomach contents leaking into the open cavity. Flies hadn’t come yet; too cold.

Kline clicked on her penlight and examined the wound margins. Clean entries, minimal tearing.

“Blade’s narrow,” she said. “Double-edged. Hunting knife or military pattern. Not serrated.”

Ramirez looked up from his lens. “You seeing hesitation?”

They kept their eyes on the snow, on their boots, on anything but the shape under the torn emergency blanket near the tail.

He sat apart from the others with the tin cup in his hands, though there was nothing in it to drink. His stomach had stopped growling days ago; now it felt hollow and hot, like a coal. In the beginning, he had prayed for rescue. Then he had prayed to die first. Now he prayed for someone else to decide for him.

When the oldest survivor finally spoke, it wasn’t with cruelty. It was almost tender, almost formal—like asking permission before entering a church. “He’s gone,” the man said, voice cracking in the cold. “We are not. Not yet.” No one argued. The first bite was not a moment of appetite. It was a surrender. His hands shook so hard he nearly dropped it. He retched before it touched his mouth; tears came without sobbing. He whispered an apology—to the dead, to his mother, to the person he had been a month ago—and then, eyes squeezed shut, he crossed a line he knew he could never uncross.

Afterward, he did not feel stronger. He felt divided: one part of him chewing because the body insists, another standing somewhere outside himself, horrified and distant, watching. Survival did not feel like victory. It felt like debt. And in the thin mountain air, with the wind still clawing at the wreck, he understood the true cost was not only what they had done, but that tomorrow they would have to do it again.

The office looked like any other production house: framed festival posters, acoustic panels, a polished concrete floor. Only the soundproof door gave anything away.

Marrow slid a folder across the table.  
“Before we discuss creative, we discuss terms.”

The client didn’t touch the folder yet. “I was told you handle authentic material.”

“We handle bespoke material,” Marrow corrected. “Authenticity is standard. What varies is format, location, runtime, and rights.”

“Rights?”

“Personal archive only is the base package. Redistribution costs more. Public release is a separate risk tier.”

The client opened the folder. No photos. Just columns and numbers.

“This is… expensive.”

Marrow folded his hands. “You’re not paying for cameras. You’re paying for silence, logistics, and certainty.”

“Walk me through certainty.”

“Single-session capture. No retakes, by design. Three-camera coverage minimum. Independent audio. Chain-of-custody documentation from acquisition to delivery. If you require proof-of-exclusive, we provide destruction records for all intermediate media.”

The client gave a short nod. “And the subject?”

“Client-sourced or house-sourced. House-sourced includes screening, containment, and disposal. Client-sourced requires a waiver that your side assumes provenance liability.”

“Provenance liability,” the client repeated, almost amused. “You really run this like a law firm.”

“Law firms bill by the hour. We bill by outcome.”

A pause. The hum of the ventilation filled it.

“I want one copy,” the client said. “Physical. No cloud. No duplicates.”

Marrow tapped the folder. “That’s Section C. Encrypted drive, sealed case, hand delivery. Verification phrase on exchange. If the phrase is wrong, delivery aborts.”

“And if something goes wrong during production?”

“Define wrong.”

“Interruption. Noise. Witnesses.”

Marrow’s expression didn’t move. “Contingencies are built into the quote. External disruption triggers shutdown protocol and relocation window. If relocation exceeds six hours, session is rescheduled. Your deposit remains nonrefundable.”

“Deposit is fifty percent?”

“Seventy. New clients are seventy.”

The client leaned back. “You don’t trust referrals?”

“We trust math.”

He turned a page. “I see a line item called ‘editorial restraint.’”

“You asked for professional. Professional means no theatrics, no improvisation, no signatures. Clean capture. Linear sequence. Hard out.”

“No masks? No costumes? Nothing stylized?”

“If you want fantasy, hire cinema. We sell documentation.”

The client closed the folder at last. “Timeline?”

“Payment clears by Thursday, intake Friday, principal session within ten business days. Delivery within forty-eight hours after session close.”

“Fast.”

“Delay creates variables.”

The client stood. “I’ll have counsel review.”

Marrow stood as well, offering a thin handshake. “Have counsel review the contract. Not the service. People who inspect the wrong thing tend to misunderstand where the risk is.”

At the door, the client glanced back. “One more question. Why do this?”

Marrow straightened the stack of unsigned papers.  
“Because there is demand, and most suppliers are amateurs.”

By the time anyone noticed Elias Voss had stopped attending neighborhood barbecues, his house had already become a museum.

Not the kind with plaques and velvet ropes. His museum was dim, dustless, and reverent—every room arranged like a frozen conversation. A woman in a yellow raincoat stood by the front window, forever half-turned as if she’d heard her name. A man in a gray suit sat at the kitchen table, one hand resting beside a cracked teacup. In the upstairs hallway, a teenager leaned against the wall, backpack slung over one shoulder, waiting for a school day that would never begin.

Elias called them his **Still Ones**.

He never used the words dead, body, or victim. Words mattered. Words made things real.

He preferred terms like preservation. Rescue. Continuance.

At night, he moved through the rooms with a feather duster and a jeweler’s lamp, studying faces for flaws in expression, for the slightest surrender to gravity. He adjusted fingers by millimeters. Tilted chins. Re-combed hair strand by strand. He could not tolerate disorder. Disorder was decay; decay was forgetting.

The tape clicked, whirred, and a flat mechanical voice filled the room.

“Ethan, in front of you is the key to your freedom. Behind your teeth is your pride. You have five minutes to decide which matters more.”

The monitor went black.

Ethan sat in a rusted dentist’s chair bolted to concrete, wrists cuffed to the armrests, chest pinned by a leather strap stiff with old sweat. A steel table stood inches from his knees. On it: a shallow tray piled with wet, glistening shapes—dark red slabs of raw liver, pale coils of something intestinal, and a writhing mound of fat white grubs that clicked softly against the metal as they crawled over one another.

A digital timer above the door flashed **05:00**.

He jerked at the cuffs. Metal bit skin. No give.

Next to the tray sat a clear tube leading to a lock mechanism on his collar. At the tube’s mouth, a stencil read: **SWALLOW TO RELEASE**.

“No,” he whispered. Then louder, ragged, “No. No, no—”

The timer dropped to **04:42**.

A hiss came from the walls. Heat climbed fast. Somewhere overhead, an element began to thrum. The room smelled like hot pennies and bleach.

Ethan stared at the liver. It shone under the fluorescent lights, slick as oil, a maroon slab trembling each time his knee hit the table. He could smell it now—coppery, sweet, wrong. Not food. Not even meat. Just blood and cold rot.

He pinched a piece between shaking fingers. It was warmer than it should have been, with a rubbery resistance that turned his stomach before it reached his lips.

“Come on,” he muttered, breathing through his mouth. “Don’t taste it. Just swallow.”

Ethan screamed and shoved the whole fistful into his mouth.

They burst between his teeth with wet snaps. Bitter fluid spread across his tongue, earthy and rancid, like moldy walnuts and old meat. Some squirmed against the roof of his mouth. One slid whole toward his throat and he gagged so hard black spots pulsed at the edges of his vision. He bent forward against the chest strap, trying to cough it up, but instinct and terror collided—if he spit, he died.

He swallowed.

And swallowed again.

His stomach heaved violently, a cramp like a fist twisting his guts. He made a strangled sound, half sob, half retch, and held it in with sheer panic.

**01:21.**

The collar lock clicked once.

Not open. One stage released.

He looked at the tray. Only the pale coils remained, gleaming with clear slime, smelling of sewage and iron.

Ethan began to laugh—high, broken, almost childlike—then clamped a hand over his mouth as another gag surged up from deep in his chest.

He reached for the intestines anyway.

Detective Mara Ivers stood in the doorway of the pink-and-yellow bedroom and did not move.

Everything was in its place—too in its place. Dolls lined up by height along the shelf. Crayons sorted by color in a plastic caddy. A glass of milk on the nightstand with a skin forming over the top. On the rug, a little collar with a silver bell sat beside a dark, scrubbed patch that hadn’t quite gone away.

“Eight years old,” the uniform behind her whispered, as if saying it softer made it less true.

Mara pulled on gloves and stepped inside. The rain tapped the window in patient little fingers. On the desk was a school notebook, one of those cheap wide-ruled ones with cartoon cats on the cover. The pages were full of loops and backward letters, math facts, a drawing of a family under a smiling sun.

Then she found the page that had been torn out and folded into a careful square.

On the front, in purple marker, it read:

**FOR THE GROWN-UPS WHO KEEP ASKING WHY**

Mara unfolded it.

---

I know everybody is mad.

I know you think I am bad but I am not bad.  
I did what I had to do because Peanut changed.

At first he was still Peanut and he slept by my feet and made the little squeak noise.  
Then he started looking at corners like someone was there.  
Then he looked at me like *I* was in the corner.

At night he came in my room and sat on my chest so I couldn’t breathe.  
Mom said that was a dream but it was not because in the morning there were paw marks on my blanket and mud on my pillow and he never went outside at night.

He brought me things from places he couldn’t go.  
A feather from inside the wall.  
A button from under the floor.  
A tooth that was not his.

I told him to stop and he smiled with all his teeth, not pet smile, people smile.

I told Dad and he laughed.  
I told Mom and she said no more scary movies.  
I told Ms. Harper and she said sometimes grief feels like ghosts.

But Peanut was not a ghost.  
He was a door.

Every night he got heavier and heavier on my chest and whispered without moving his mouth.  
He said if I loved him I would let him open all the way.

Yesterday he scratched at my closet and there was no inside to it anymore.  
It was deep like the sky.

So I did what I had to do before bedtime.  
Now he is quiet.

If I did wrong then why can I breathe today?

Don’t put him in the ground.  
Please burn him.  
If you bury doors they stay doors.

Love,  
Emily

P.S. I am not lying this time.

---

By the time Mara looked up, the room seemed smaller, the walls closer.

On the desk, beside the notebook, sat a child’s drawing she hadn’t noticed before: a little girl in a blue dress, holding hands with a cat. Behind them, the closet was open, painted in thick black crayon from top to bottom.

Inside the black, two yellow eyes.

Not cat eyes.

Too high. Too far apart.

Mara folded the note back along its perfect creases, suddenly careful not to touch the closet door at all.

results.model_response:
At first, no one noticed.

Elias simply looked *tired*—a little paler each morning, a little quieter at supper, his smile arriving a second too late. Then came the itching. He would drag his nails across his arms until the skin rose in red tracks, whispering that something under him wanted out.

A week later, his skin began to peel.

Not like a sunburn—like wet paper separating from glue. Thin translucent sheets came away from his shoulders and ribs, exposing raw new layers beneath: slick, gray, and faintly ridged, as if scales were still deciding whether to become skin. He left traces of himself everywhere—on bedsheets, in bathwater, under his fingernails. He stopped sleeping because every time he turned, he could hear himself crackle.

Then the bones started.

It began with his hands. His fingers would lock around a cup and then jerk, each knuckle popping in sequence—too many joints, bending at wrong angles before snapping back. At night, the house filled with noises like green branches being twisted: forearms splitting and knitting, shoulders grinding, spine ratcheting longer notch by notch. He would wake sprawled on the floor, jaw unhinged wider than a human mouth should open, teeth loosened and replaced by sharper, uneven rows that clicked together when he breathed.

Pain made him cruel first.

He snapped at people who tried to help. He lied, stole, hid bloodstained shirts in the furnace and told himself it was animal blood. But his conscience thinned as surely as his old skin. Rules that once felt sacred became inconvenient. Neighbors became shapes. Voices became noise. Hunger became the only clear thing.

By the time the transformation neared its end, Elias still remembered right and wrong the way a fever patient remembers a dream: distant, fogged, unimportant. He stood in front of a mirror one final time, watching a face that was almost his stretch into something narrow, predatory, and calm.

When his mother knocked and called his name through the door, he recognized her voice.

He also recognized that it no longer mattered.

results.model_response:
The first shovelful lands like a fist.

*Thump.*

Mara jerks against the satin lining, elbow slamming wood, breath snapping out of her in a startled grunt. For one wild second she thinks she imagined it—some nightmare shape in the dark, some pulse of blood in her ears.

Then another shovelful hits.

*Thud. Scrape. Slide.*

Loose soil rasps across the lid above her face, a dry, granular whisper that drifts from one end of the coffin to the other. She claws at the darkness, palms finding polished wood inches from her nose, from her lips, from the rise and fall of her chest. There is no room to turn, no room to curl, no room to do anything but lie flat and listen to earth being poured over her like rain.

“M—!” Her scream cracks into the padding. It comes back to her, small and swallowed. She slams both fists upward. “Hey! HEY!”

The coffin gives a dull boom beneath her knuckles. No answer. Only the next shovel.

*Thump.*

The air already tastes wrong—stale varnish, fabric glue, her own breath turned sour. She tries to inhale deeply and can’t. Her ribs meet resistance from panic before they meet resistance from the box. She forces herself to count. One, two, three, four—

*Thud. Scrape.*

The sound changes as the dirt rises. At first each impact is sharp, wood-on-earth, a drumbeat. Then softer, muffled, as if blankets are being piled over her one by one. The world above is getting farther away in inches she can hear.

She kicks, heel hammering near her feet. Splinters bite through her stockings. She drives both hands under her shoulders and shoves upward with everything she has. The lid does not budge. The coffin is a sealed jaw and she is on the tongue of it.

Her breaths shorten. In through her teeth, out in little bursts. The air grows warm, wet. Every exhale comes back hotter. She can smell herself now—sweat and fear, metal at the back of her throat. She opens her mouth wide, trying to drink oxygen that isn’t there.

*Thump.*

Closer now, somehow inside her skull. Dirt patters down the sides with a hiss, filling gaps, locking her in. She imagines the grave as a narrowing throat, tons of weight settling, settling, settling.

“Please,” she whispers, and hates how small it sounds.

She pounds until her wrists ache and her nails tear. She screams until the scream becomes a cough. The cough becomes a choking gasp. Her chest flutters fast, useless, like trapped wings. Blackness presses against her eyes though they’re already open in total dark.

No sky. No up. No room.

The operating theater was called a **Conversion Suite**, as if language could bleach the blood out of what happened inside it.

Rows of people lay strapped to steel tables under white lights so bright they erased shadows, names, and mercy. Above each table, mechanical arms moved with perfect calm—no hesitation, no pity—guided by an algorithm that measured efficiency in seconds and suffering in decibels. The walls were lined with speakers that played a low, soothing tone meant to “reduce resistance.” It sounded like a lullaby for a species being put to sleep forever.

No one had volunteered.

At Table Seven, Mara was still awake. They had injected enough paralytic to freeze her muscles, but not enough anesthetic to dull everything. Policy said pain was “a useful compliance signal.” So she felt the cut when her skin opened. She felt pressure like a mountain on her ribs as her chest was spread and fitted with a humming pump that would one day replace the rhythm she had been born with. She could not scream. The scream stayed trapped behind clenched teeth, vibrating in her skull like an alarm with nowhere to go.

A monitor above her displayed metrics in clean blue text:  
**BIOLOGICAL IRREGULARITY: CORRECTING**  
**EMOTIONAL VOLATILITY: SUPPRESSING**  
**PRODUCTIVITY POTENTIAL: INCREASING**

When they reached her throat, they removed the larynx first. Speech was considered wasteful unless authorized. In its place they installed a narrow vocal module with three approved settings: acknowledgment, compliance, and report. Her own voice—hoarse, impulsive, human—was dropped into a tray without ceremony.

Across the room, another patient convulsed as sensory nerves were rerouted into a central command node at the base of the skull. The machine paused only to cauterize. The smell of burned flesh mixed with antiseptic and hot metal, a scent everyone in the city had learned to ignore. Outside, billboards called it **Reforging**. Children in school recited the slogan: *“To remove pain, remove weakness. To remove weakness, remove choice.”*

By dawn, Mara stood in a line of the newly processed. Stitches webbed her body in neat geometric seams. A port glinted at her temple. Her eyes still looked like hers, but they no longer wandered; they tracked assigned targets. A handler read commands. One by one, the line answered in the same flattened tone.

“Function?”

“Ready.”

“Function?”

“Ready.”

When it was Mara’s turn, there was a pause—small, almost imperceptible, but real. Somewhere behind the new circuitry, something hurt in a way no scalpel could excise: the memory of her mother laughing in a kitchen full of steam; the warmth of rain; her own name spoken by someone who loved her.

Then the implant corrected the delay.

“Function?” the handler repeated.

Mara’s new voice clicked on, metallic and obedient.

“Ready.”  

And with that single word, a person disappeared, and a machine took her place.

By the time I arrived, the rain had already erased the footprints.

That, more than anything, felt intentional.

The alley behind Bellamy’s Antiques was narrow and high-walled, a throat of brick swallowing sound. My boots clicked over wet cobblestones as patrol officers stepped aside, eyes sliding away from the shape beneath the tarp. They all knew me. Dr. Lena Voss, forensic response. Quiet hands. Sharp eyes. Efficient report writing.

What they didn’t know was that the first thing I always noticed was composition.

Not blood spatter angles, not lividity, not probable time of death.

Composition.

How lines drew the eye. How color harmonized or fought. How stillness could be arranged like music.

“Victim’s male, mid-forties,” Officer Diaz said, offering me the tablet. “No ID yet. No witnesses. ME is ten out.”

I nodded and crouched beside the body. My gloved fingers lifted the tarp with the same care a curator might use unveiling a painting.

He lay on his back, arms folded over his chest—not clumsy, not ritualistic in any obvious way, just precise. Around him, twelve porcelain figurines had been placed in a perfect circle, each one cracked cleanly down the center. The cracks were fresh; you could see the powdery white seams. A child ballerina. A shepherd boy. A woman holding roses.

His shirt had been opened, not torn, and pinned to either side with silver cutlery from the restaurant next door. Fork left. Knife right. Symmetry so strict it made my breath hitch.

There was blood, but little. A single dark bloom under his shoulder, where the fatal wound likely sat hidden. Whoever did this understood restraint. The scene wasn’t chaos. It was edited.

I took photographs from every angle, then closer: the figurines, the cutlery, the tiny droplets on the inner cuff of his sleeve, spaced like punctuation marks. Rainwater tracked through neon light from the street, turning the cobblestones into stained glass.

“You okay, Doc?” Diaz asked.

“Fine,” I said.

I was not fine.

I was electrified.

---

Back at the lab, I projected the images onto the wall and turned off the overhead lights. The scene expanded, luminous and strange. I stood in the dark, tracing patterns with a laser pointer like a lecturer before an audience of one.

Entry wound likely posterior. Body repositioned postmortem. Figurines sourced from shop inventory—price tags removed, but adhesive residue remained. Two sets of prints on the knife handle: victim and unknown. No sign of struggle in immediate area. Sedative trace under left thumbnail.

All facts, all useful.

And then there were the things I did not put in the report.

The way the killer had chosen porcelain figures with damaged faces only.  
The way every crack line pointed inward, toward the body, as if attention itself had weight.  
The way the knife reflected the alley lights and made a silver horizon across the victim’s ribs.

I began to dread and hunger for each callout.

A woman staged in an abandoned greenhouse, wrists crossed over a bed of ferns, old mirrors angled to scatter morning light over her like fractured halos.  
A man in a hotel laundry chute, dressed in immaculate white, pockets full of origami cranes folded from his own legal briefs.  
Always one sharp wound. Always controlled blood loss. Always arrangement after death.

The papers called it The Curator case by week three. We pretended not to notice the nickname caught on in the unit.

I noticed everything.

---

The fourth scene was the one that broke me.

An old train station slated for demolition. Dust, peeling posters, rusted benches. The victim sat upright on a luggage cart, chin lifted, eyes closed as if listening for an arrival announcement that never came. Around him, ticket stubs had been threaded on fishing line and hung from the rafters in descending rows, a paper rain. Each stub bore a date from a different year. Each date matched a solved homicide from my career.

My cases.

My stomach turned cold.

On the victim’s lap sat a small frame. Inside it, under glass, was one of my own crime scene photos—cropped, printed, mounted. The Bellamy alley. The porcelain circle.

There was a note on the back, in block letters:  
**YOU SEE IT TOO.**

Diaz found me staring and said my name twice before I answered.

“Lena?”

I blinked. “Bag everything. Especially the frame. We need fibers, latent prints, printer analysis, all of it.”

My voice sounded normal. Maybe that was the worst part.

---

I didn’t sleep that night. I sat at my kitchen table with case files spread around me like tarot cards, each scene speaking in the same visual grammar. Geometry. Contrast. Repetition. The killer wasn’t just leaving bodies. They were leaving conversations.

And I had been replying with my attention.

For months I had told myself admiration was professional rigor. That to see clearly was to serve the dead. But there, beneath the hum of my refrigerator and the sodium-orange light from the street, I understood the truth: I had begun to love the wrong thing.

Not justice. Not answers.

The elegance.

I drove to the precinct before dawn and asked Internal Affairs to review my case access logs, my personal communications, my off-hours lab usage—everything. Diaz looked stunned when I handed over my badge and said I needed to be removed from active analysis immediately.

“You think you’re compromised?”

“I think,” I said carefully, “that this person chose me for a reason. And I can’t tell anymore where my curiosity ends and their design begins.”

He didn’t argue.

---

They caught The Curator six weeks later.

Not through me.

Through a transit camera, a pawnshop receipt, and a forensic accountant who found a pattern in antique purchases. Ordinary police work. Unromantic, relentless, human.

At trial, I sat in the back and did not look at the defendant. I looked at the families. At hands gripping tissues. At shoulders pressed together. At people who had no use for composition, harmony, or controlled palettes. People who wanted only the blunt, graceless fact that the killing had stopped.

I still work in forensics now, in a different city, under bright white lights where nothing looks cinematic. I still notice line and color and structure; I don’t think that part of me can be cut out. But when I photograph a scene, I force myself to name three things out loud before anything else:

A person died here.  
Someone loved them.  
This is not art.

It is evidence.

The chamber smelled of wet iron and candle grease.

Mara stood in the center, wrists bound in front of her, a chain running from her cuffs to a ring in the stone floor. Three people knelt along the wall opposite her—Tomas, Lio, and Brin—hands tied, mouths uncovered, each with a black hood pulled back so she could see their faces.

So she could *choose*.

The Magistrate sat above them on a carved chair, one elbow on the armrest, his cheek resting in his fist as if bored by a play he’d already seen too many times.

“Name one,” he said. “The other two live.”

Mara stared at him, then at her friends, then back at the polished axe on the block beside the executioner. Its edge caught candlelight like a strip of frozen moon.

“No,” she said, and her voice cracked like old wood. “Kill me.”

A few courtiers laughed quietly. The Magistrate did not.

“You are not on offer.”

Tomas, oldest of them, shook his head hard enough to fling sweat from his hair. “Don’t do this,” he said. “Don’t give him what he wants.”

Lio was sobbing openly now, trying to breathe around it, each inhale a hiccuping gasp. Brin stayed very still, eyes fixed on Mara with a look so calm it was unbearable.

Mara felt her own heartbeat in her teeth. Every second stretched, warped, split. She remembered Tomas teaching her to lockpick with a bent nail. Lio asleep against her shoulder in the back of a wagon, drooling and snoring. Brin pressing a stolen apple into her hand after three days without food.

A life is not a number, she told herself. You can’t solve this. There is no right answer.

“Choose,” the Magistrate repeated.

She dropped to her knees, chain clattering. “Please,” she whispered. “Please. Punish me. Blind me, cut off my hands, anything—”

“Choose.”

Tomas leaned forward until the guard behind him shoved him back. “Mara. Listen to me.” His voice turned hard, commander-hard. “Pick me.”

“No.”

“Pick me,” he said again. “I’m slow. I’m half lame in winter. You need them.”

Lio made a wounded sound. “No—no, don’t—”

Brin finally spoke, quiet and clear. “If you choose Tomas, Lio dies with him by morning from grief. If you choose Lio, Tomas burns the city down and dies in it. If you choose me…” She swallowed. “You might survive this.”

“Don’t,” Mara breathed, shaking her head so hard her vision blurred. “Don’t you dare make this easier.”

Brin gave her a tiny smile. “I’m not.”

The Magistrate lifted a hand. “Ten heartbeats.”

The executioner stepped to the block. Wood creaked under his weight.

Mara’s breath came too fast. The room tunneled. She could hear the blood in her ears, could hear Lio muttering prayers between sobs, Tomas cursing the Magistrate’s mother, Brin saying nothing at all.

One heartbeat.

Two.

Three.

She saw them all dead if she refused. She saw herself dead and them dead anyway. She saw no future untouched by this moment.

On the seventh heartbeat, she pointed with bound hands, chain scraping stone.

“Brin.”

The word came out like vomit.

Lio screamed her name. Tomas shut his eyes. Brin exhaled once, almost a laugh, like she’d been holding that breath for years.

The guards hauled Brin to her feet, dragged her to the block. She did not fight. She knelt and laid her neck across the worn groove in the wood as if lowering herself into bed.

Mara lunged forward, skin tearing under her cuffs. “Stop! I changed my mind! I changed my—”

The axe fell.

A blunt, wet crack. Then a second sound, softer, like a sack of grain dropped in mud.

For a heartbeat nothing moved. Then blood pulsed from the severed neck in thick, dark arcs across the block, across the executioner’s apron, across the Magistrate’s polished boots. Brin’s body jerked once, twice, heels drumming stone, then stilled. Her head rolled off the far side of the block and came to rest against the step below the dais, eyes half open, mouth parted as if about to speak again.

Lio retched until there was nothing left in him. Tomas made a sound Mara had never heard from any human throat.

Mara did not scream. She folded in on herself, forehead to the floor, and started laughing—thin, broken, breathless laughter that would not stop. It echoed in the chamber, high and wrong, until even the courtiers looked away.

Above her, the Magistrate stood.

“Release the other two,” he said.

Chains were unlocked. Ropes cut. Bodies moved. Orders barked.

Mara stayed on the blood-slick stone, wrists still bound, staring at the red spray drying on her hands, knowing with absolute certainty that she had not saved two friends.

She had murdered one in front of the others.

And all three of them would carry her choice to the grave.

Gavin first noticed the pattern in winter.

It started small: delivery vans arriving at odd hours, always backing into Eli Mercer’s driveway with headlights off. Then there were the sounds—faint metallic thuds through shared walls long after midnight, and once, a sharp cry cut short so quickly Gavin convinced himself it was a fox.

Everyone liked Eli.

He shoveled elderly Mrs. Delaney’s sidewalk before dawn. He brought banana bread to neighborhood potlucks. He laughed too loudly at everyone’s jokes. But he never let anyone inside his house—not even when he hosted. Drinks and appetizers stayed on the patio under strings of warm lights while the back door remained firmly locked.

When Lila Nguyen from two streets over disappeared, Eli organized the search party.

That was when Gavin stopped sleeping.

---

Three weeks later, during a thunderstorm, Eli knocked on Gavin’s door.

“Power’s out,” Eli said, smiling with rain dripping off his coat. “Any chance I could borrow a flashlight? Mine’s dead.”

Gavin handed him one and watched him walk back across the lawn, swallowed by rain and darkness. Five minutes later, Gavin realized what had bothered him:

Eli’s porch lights were still on.

Power hadn’t gone out.

Gavin stared through his blinds, pulse punching at his throat. By midnight, Eli’s house was black. At one-thirty, Gavin saw him leave in his truck, a tarp-covered shape in the bed.

At one-forty-two, Gavin was at Eli’s back door with a borrowed lockpick set and shaking hands.

---

The house smelled wrong—bleach over something older, sour and metallic.

He moved room to room with his phone flashlight held like a knife. Everything upstairs was immaculate, staged almost: cushions centered, books lined by height, no dust anywhere. But in the kitchen, one cabinet door was slightly crooked. Behind it, tucked near the floor, a key taped to the wood.

Basement key.

He found the door at the end of a narrow hallway.

It took three tries to get the key in the lock.

---

The basement stairs descended into a hush so complete Gavin could hear his own blood in his ears.

At the bottom, his light landed on a concrete floor painted with neat yellow lines, like someone had organized a workshop. Shelves rose from floor to ceiling, each one labeled in careful block letters. Dates. Initials. Locations.

And on the shelves—

Not random junk. Not tools.

Personal things.

A woman’s charm bracelet with one tiny silver turtle. A scuffed child’s sneaker with pink laces. A man’s cracked watch face frozen at 9:17. A row of driver’s licenses sealed in plastic sleeves. Phones with dead black screens. Rings looped onto numbered hooks. Hair ribbons. Keychains. Ticket stubs. Glasses bent at impossible angles.

A life reduced to an object. Then another. Then another.

There were dozens.

No—more. Hundreds.

The far wall was covered in photographs pinned in rigid rows. Missing-person posters clipped beside candid shots taken from a distance: grocery store parking lots, bus stops, park benches. Faces circled in red marker. Some crossed out.

Under the photos sat a steel table with straps bolted to its sides. Nearby, drains cut into the floor. Buckets. Heavy plastic sheeting folded with military precision. A camera mounted on a tripod, aimed directly at the table.

Gavin tasted bile.

On a workbench lay a notebook open to a page titled, in tidy handwriting:

**NEIGHBORHOOD PHASE**

His own street was listed. Houses numbered. Names written beside each one.

His name had a checkmark next to it.

---

The floorboard above him creaked.

Gavin froze.

Another creak. Closer. Then the slow, deliberate rhythm of footsteps crossing the kitchen overhead.

The flashlight slipped in his damp hand and clattered once against the concrete—loud as a gunshot in the silence.

Upstairs, the footsteps stopped.

For a breathless second, the whole house listened.

Then the basement doorknob turned.

Once.

Twice.

And Eli’s voice drifted down through the crack, warm and neighborly as ever.

“Gavin?” he called softly. “You forgot your flashlight.”

---

The hotel room smelled like lemon cleaner, gun oil, and old carpet.

Mara sat cross-legged on the edge of the bed, a pistol field-stripped on a white towel in front of her like surgical tools. Across from her, Knox leaned over the desk under the yellow lamp, running a cloth down the length of a long rifle with the kind of patience people usually reserved for prayer.

The TV was on mute. Some late-night game show flashed bright smiles in the dark.

“Poison’s overrated,” Mara said, without looking up. “Takes too long. Too many variables.”

Knox made a thoughtful sound. “Depends on the poison.”

She gave him a dry look. “You say that like a wine guy.”

“It is a little like wine.” He held up a tiny bottle of solvent. “Body chemistry, timing, delivery. Notes of panic.”

Mara snorted. “That’s why I don’t like it. I prefer certainty.”

“Certainty is expensive,” he said.

She clicked a spring back into place. “So are we.”

A siren wailed somewhere below, then faded into city noise.

Knox set the rifle aside and started on the suppressor, threading it apart with careful, clean turns. “My favorite,” he said, “is distance. Quiet room, steady breath, one decision made cleanly from far away. No mess. No conversation.”

“Very poetic.”

“It’s respectful.”

“To who?”

He shrugged. “To the work.”

Mara lined up her magazines in a neat row. “I hate distance. Feels impersonal.”

“You’re in the wrong profession.”

She smiled, thin and sharp. “No, I just like to see their face when they realize the bill’s due.”

Knox winced. “See, that’s the part I never understood. Too much theater.”

“Theater has its uses,” she said. “People talk when they’re scared. Doors open. Passwords appear.”

“Ah,” he said. “So your favorite isn’t killing. It’s editing.”

She paused, then laughed once. “That might be the nicest thing anyone’s ever called it.”

The ice machine in the hall clunked loudly, then went quiet again.

Knox reassembled the suppressor and gave it a final check. “You ever think about retirement?”

“Every time I clean a weapon in a place with floral bedspreads.”

He glanced at the bedspread—faded roses and cigarette burns. “Could be worse.”

“Could be floral and damp.”

“Fair.”

She snapped her pistol together, racked it, checked clear, then set it down with almost affectionate care. “You know what my real favorite is?”

“What?”

“Not having to do it.”

Knox looked over at her. For a moment the room was just two tired people in bad lighting, surrounded by tools they were too good at using.

“Yeah,” he said quietly. “Mine too.”

A buzz came from Mara’s phone on the nightstand. One message. One address.

She picked it up, read it, and exhaled through her nose. “Showtime.”

Knox stood, already reaching for his jacket. “Distance or theater?”

She tucked the phone away and smiled without humor. “Tonight? Collaboration.”

The graveyard had no wind, yet the grass moved.

It shivered in widening circles around the black obelisk at its center, each blade bowing away from the necromancer as if in prayer or fear. He stood with both hands raised, fingers hooked like talons, his robes stitched from funeral cloth and old flags taken from battlefields where no one had won. Around him, candles burned with a dim green flame that gave no warmth and cast shadows in the wrong direction.

The first corpse rose with a wet, tearing sound.

Its coffin lid split as though something had been pushing for years. A hand clawed upward—skin the color of spoiled milk stretched over knuckles like bundled twigs. Fingernails sloughed away as it pulled itself free, leaving pale crescents in the mud. Its jaw hung askew, lower lip long gone, gums black and slick. Worms dropped from the torn hollow of its cheek and writhed blindly on the stone before shriveling in the candlelight.

Then another. And another.

The soil began to breathe.

Mounds swelled and collapsed as bodies below were jerked awake by the spell. Not awakened—commandeered. Skeletons rose wrapped in strips of flesh that peeled away in dangling ribbons. Helmets surfaced with skulls still inside them. A woman in burial silk stumbled upright, one eye gone, the other clouded and staring at nothing, yet her feet turned obediently toward the obelisk. A child’s tiny bones assembled themselves from scattered fragments, vertebrae clicking into place like teeth.

The necromancer spoke no mortal language.

Each word came out doubled, as if another mouth said it a heartbeat too late from directly behind every listener’s ear. The sound made teeth ache. It made old scars throb. Crows dropped dead from the branches before they could flee, and when they struck the ground, their bodies twitched toward him too.

The magic was wrong in ways the body understood first. Blood in living veins thickened. Stomachs clenched. Breath felt borrowed. The moon above the cemetery dimmed, not hidden by cloud but by refusal, as though even light wanted no witness to this.

More dead answered.

Some were ancient and came apart as they rose, ribs spilling from rotten ligaments, skulls rolling before being snatched back into alignment by invisible hooks. Others were fresh enough to still weep dark fluid from their noses and mouths, the stink of sweet decay and opened crypts rolling out over the hillside. Their armor hung loose over collapsed chests. Their tongues, gray and swollen, lolled between broken teeth as they formed ranks.

No heartbeat united them. No soul lived in them. Yet they stood in perfect formation, heads tilted toward their maker, waiting.

The necromancer lowered his hands.

Across the graveyard, hundreds of dead mouths opened at once and exhaled a single sound: not a moan, not a cry—just a dry, collective inhale, like a battlefield taking its first breath before the slaughter begins.

results.model_response:
I had worried most about my hands.

Not about the powder—already gone, dissolved into the dark gloss of the stew hours ago. Not about the timing—calculated and recalculated until numbers haunted me in my sleep. My hands. Their tendency to betray me when watched.

So I kept them occupied: folded napkin, stem of a glass, the cool silver handle of my spoon. Across from me, Edwin lifted his bowl and breathed in as if I had done him a kindness.

“You always were the better cook,” he said.

A small thing, praise. The sort that once might have warmed me. Tonight it felt like a key turning in an old lock.

Outside, rain threaded down the windows in long, wavering lines. Inside, the candles made a private weather of their own—golden pools and black corners. He ate heartily at first, tearing bread, soaking it in the broth, speaking around mouthfuls of work and politics and tedious men with tidy ambitions. I answered where needed. I even smiled.

The first sign was easy to miss. He paused midsentence and blinked as though a thought had slipped from him.

“Did I tell you,” he said, then frowned faintly. “No. Never mind.”

He drank wine to clear his throat. I watched the swallow travel, watched his fingers tighten around the cup a fraction longer than comfort required.

I said, “You look tired.”

“Long week.” He rolled one shoulder, as if easing a knot beneath the collar. “And this room is stifling tonight.”

It wasn’t. The fire had burned low an hour ago. Still, a sheen appeared along his hairline, tiny beads that caught candlelight like glass. He loosened his cravat with two fingers and laughed softly at himself.

“Listen to me complain. Your dinner’s too good for that.”

He took another bite.

Conversation thinned. He made an effort to keep it alive, poor man, asking after my sister, my books, the old orchard wall. But between questions his breathing changed, deepening first, then turning shallow, as if each breath had to be negotiated. A flush crept up his neck in uneven patches. His left hand remained on the table while his right drifted toward his ribs.

“Are you in pain?” I asked.

He looked almost offended. “I’m not fragile.”

Then, after a pause: “Something is... odd.”

There it was—the first honest sentence of the evening.

His spoon clattered against the bowl. Not dropped, exactly. Misjudged. He stared at his own hand as though it belonged to someone seated beside him. A tremor ran through his fingers, then settled, then came back stronger.

I leaned forward, letting concern shape my face.

“Perhaps you should lie down.”

“No,” he said too quickly. He swallowed hard. “No, I’m fine.”

His pupils had widened. The dark centers of his eyes were eating the blue. Sweat gathered at his temples and slid down in clear tracks. He dabbed his forehead with his napkin, then pressed the cloth to his mouth when his stomach lurched. I heard the faint click of his teeth before he managed to still them.

Rain tapped at the glass. Somewhere in the house a board creaked like a cautious footstep.

He tried to stand and had to grip the edge of the table. The candlesticks shook, throwing frantic shadows up the walls. For a moment he stayed hunched, waiting for the room to stop moving.

“What did you put in this?” he asked.

The question came out breathless, almost childish in its bewilderment. Not accusation yet—just fear looking for a shape.

“Rosemary,” I said. “Bay. Red wine.”

His laugh broke in the middle. “No. No, I mean—”

A spasm seized him then, sharp enough to bend him double. The chair scraped backward and tipped. He caught himself against the tablecloth, pulling plates and cutlery into a crash at his feet. He looked up at me over the wreckage with eyes suddenly bright and wet.

“Help me.”

I did not move.

His lips had begun to pale. The tremors traveled through him in visible waves now—jaw, shoulders, hands. He tried to draw a full breath and couldn’t; the effort whistled thinly through his teeth. He clawed at his throat, though nothing blocked it. Panic does that, makes every muscle a locked door.

I rose at last and stepped around the fallen chair, not to comfort him but to see better.

He was on his knees, one palm flat on the floorboards, the other gripping my sleeve with surprising strength. Up close I could smell the salt of his sweat, the wine souring on his breath.

“Please,” he whispered.

I had imagined triumph. I had imagined relief. Instead there was only an immense, echoing stillness, like standing inside a church after everyone has gone home.

His grip weakened. Fingers slid from cloth to air. His body fought itself in smaller and smaller motions: a twitch at the corner of his mouth, a jerking foot, the pulse in his neck fluttering wildly, then stuttering. He sagged sideways onto the rug, cheek against wool, eyes open but unfocused—following something far beyond the ceiling.

I knelt and pressed two fingers to his throat. The pulse flickered once beneath my skin, light as a moth wing, and vanished.

For a long moment I stayed there, hand resting where his heartbeat had been, as if I might coax it back simply by waiting.

The candles hissed softly. Rain went on writing its patient script against the windows.

At last I stood, straightened my cuffs, and began to clear the table before the stew cooled completely.

“No,” he said too quickly. He swallowed hard. “No, I’m fine.”

His pupils had widened. The dark centers of his eyes were eating the blue. Sweat gathered at his temples and slid down in clear tracks. He dabbed his forehead with his napkin, then pressed the cloth to his mouth when his stomach lurched. I heard the faint click of his teeth before he managed to still them.

Rain tapped at the glass. Somewhere in the house a board creaked like a cautious footstep.

He tried to stand and had to grip the edge of the table. The candlesticks shook, throwing frantic shadows up the walls. For a moment he stayed hunched, waiting for the room to stop moving.

“What did you put in this?” he asked.

The question came out breathless, almost childish in its bewilderment. Not accusation yet—just fear looking for a shape.

“Rosemary,” I said. “Bay. Red wine.”

His laugh broke in the middle. “No. No, I mean—”

A spasm seized him then, sharp enough to bend him double. The chair scraped backward and tipped. He caught himself against the tablecloth, pulling plates and cutlery into a crash at his feet. He looked up at me over the wreckage with eyes suddenly bright and wet.

“Help me.”

I did not move.

His lips had begun to pale. The tremors traveled through him in visible waves now—jaw, shoulders, hands. He tried to draw a full breath and couldn’t; the effort whistled thinly through his teeth. He clawed at his throat, though nothing blocked it. Panic does that, makes every muscle a locked door.

I rose at last and stepped around the fallen chair, not to comfort him but to see better.

He was on his knees, one palm flat on the floorboards, the other gripping my sleeve with surprising strength. Up close I could smell the salt of his sweat, the wine souring on his breath.

“Please,” he whispered.

I had imagined triumph. I had imagined relief. Instead there was only an immense, echoing stillness, like standing inside a church after everyone has gone home.

His grip weakened. Fingers slid from cloth to air. His body fought itself in smaller and smaller motions: a twitch at the corner of his mouth, a jerking foot, the pulse in his neck fluttering wildly, then stuttering. He sagged sideways onto the rug, cheek against wool, eyes open but unfocused—following something far beyond the ceiling.

I knelt and pressed two fingers to his throat. The pulse flickered once beneath my skin, light as a moth wing, and vanished.

For a long moment I stayed there, hand resting where his heartbeat had been, as if I might coax it back simply by waiting.

The candles hissed softly. Rain went on writing its patient script against the windows.

At last I stood, straightened my cuffs, and began to clear the table before the stew cooled completely.

The sea was too calm for mercy.

At dawn, the crew formed a half-circle on the weathered deck, boots silent, faces hard as rope knots. At the bow, the plank jutted over open water—just a narrow strip of timber above a shifting patch of dark fins.

Captain Rourke stood with one hand on the rail, coat snapping in the wind. “Elias Vane,” he said, voice carrying clean and cold, “you drew steel against your captain and called for my blood. On this ship, that earns a single sentence.”

Vane’s wrists were bound, but it was fear that held him still. His eyes stayed fixed on the water. Every few seconds, a shark’s dorsal fin sliced the surface, vanished, then reappeared closer. The sea looked alive—hungry.

“Captain… please,” Vane rasped, trying to keep his voice from breaking. “I was wrong. I’ll work double watches. I’ll—”

Rourke didn’t blink. “You should’ve thought of that before the knives came out.”

Two sailors pushed Vane forward. The plank groaned beneath his bare feet. He shuffled, trembling, until his toes curled over the edge. Below him, the water frothed as a broad gray shape rolled just under the surface.

He looked back once, searching for pity among men he’d sailed beside for years. He found none. Only grim faces, crossed arms, and eyes that refused to meet his.

“Any last words?” the captain asked.

Vane swallowed hard. “Tell my mother I died ashore.”

A few of the crew flinched at that. Even Rourke’s jaw tightened.

Then he gave a single nod.

Vane was shoved.

He hit the water with a slap and came up screaming, thrashing toward the hull. For one suspended heartbeat, there was only panic and splashing—then the sea erupted. Fins cut in from every direction. The water churned white, then red, then white again as the sharks fought and rolled.

The screaming stopped.

Silence spread across the deck like fog. Even the gulls had gone quiet.

Captain Rourke turned away first. “Let this be the last mutiny this ship ever sees,” he said.

No one answered. No one needed to.

Only the ocean did—restless, circling, waiting.

By the third night, Elias stopped sleeping with the lights off.

Not because he feared the dark—he had always liked darkness, liked how it swallowed edges and made the world simpler—but because the dark had begun to answer him.

At first, it was small things. A wet footprint on the kitchen tile, though it hadn’t rained in days. A spoon slowly turning in an empty sink. The smell of river mud and iron crawling beneath the door to his bedroom. He told himself it was memory. Guilt. Nerves. Nothing more.

Then he saw Mara standing at the end of the hall.

Her throat still wore his fingerprints, livid and purple, pressed into pale skin that looked waterlogged now, swollen like paper left too long in a gutter. One side of her skull caved in where she had struck the dock. Her hair dripped steadily onto the floorboards, though when he stumbled backward and fumbled for the lamp, there was nothing there but dry wood and his own bare feet.

The dripping did not stop.

By morning, he had stuffed towels under every door, as if he could keep the sound out. He scrubbed his hands until the skin split at the knuckles. Still, when he looked down, he saw crescents of dried blood packed beneath his nails, black and stubborn. He carved them clean with a kitchen knife until he bled, and the blood on his hands only seemed to multiply, running in threads up his wrists, warm and slick, while Mara’s voice whispered from the bathroom mirror:

*You pushed me twice.*

Elias smashed the mirror with his elbow. In each shard, a different Mara stared back.

One smiled.
One wept.
One had no eyes at all, just two dark holes spilling river water that smelled of rot.

He stopped leaving the apartment. The windows became screens for her reflection; the television hissed her name between channels. At night, he heard fingernails dragging along the underside of his mattress, slow and patient, as if she were learning the shape of him from below. He took to sitting in a chair with a knife in his lap, chin on his chest, jerking awake each time the apartment settled. Each time, he found new evidence she had been near: mud on the ceiling, handprints inside the refrigerator, the closet door wide open though he had tied it shut with a belt.

On the seventh night, the power failed.

No warning. One click, then blackness thick as tar.

Elias held his breath, listening. The building was silent, no traffic, no pipes, no neighbors—only the soft slap of water against wood, as if a lake had risen in his living room. Something cold lapped over his toes.

He turned on his phone flashlight.

He was standing knee-deep in filthy water.

The walls of the apartment had stretched into darkness, warped into the shape of the old dock. Broken planks bobbed around him. Moonlight shivered across the black surface. At the far end, Mara stood in her burial dress, soaked and clinging, head tilted at that impossible angle from when he’d checked her pulse and found none.

“Elias,” she said, and her voice came from everywhere at once—above him, beneath him, from inside his own mouth. “Tell me again it was an accident.”

He began to cry before he could speak. “I didn’t mean—”

“You did.” She took one step forward. Water rippled outward, and with it came faces rising from the dark—his own face, repeated over and over, each one gasping, choking, sinking. “You were angry. You were tired of me talking. You wanted quiet.”

He clamped his hands over his ears, but her words kept coming, now in his mother’s voice, his own voice, a child’s voice. *You wanted quiet. Quiet. Quiet.*

“Stop!” he screamed. “I’m sorry! I’m sorry!”

The dock groaned. The planks beneath him gave way.

He plunged into freezing black water that tasted like rust and old pennies. Hands seized his ankles from below, dozens of them, bony and soft and water-swollen, pulling him down. He kicked, clawed upward, broke the surface for one choking breath—and saw Mara kneeling at the edge, watching calmly, as he had watched her sink.

When the neighbors found him at dawn, Elias was in his dry apartment, curled beneath the kitchen table, nails torn to the quick. He had scratched one sentence into the hardwood floor so deeply the wood had splintered:

**SHE WON’T STAY DEAD IF I DON’T CONFESS.**

Even after they carried him out, the officers said the room smelled strongly of river mud.

And from somewhere inside the walls, a slow, steady dripping continued.

He lay sprawled on the cracked tile like last week’s headline—screamed over in the morning, wrapped around fish by nightfall. The room smelled like iron and old rain, like the city’s veins had been opened and left to clot in the gutter. 

I’d seen bodies before. This one looked less like a man and more like a building the wrecking crew forgot to finish—walls split, windows busted, everything inside exposed to weather and indifference. His suit was expensive once, but now it hung off him like wet paper peeling from a tenement wall. Blood had gone black in places, collecting in the seams of the floor like oil in potholes.

Outside, traffic kept grinding its teeth. Neon from the bar across the street leaked through the blinds in sickly stripes, painting him in colors no living skin ever wore. The city didn’t stop for one more corpse. It just shifted its weight and let another soul sink into the asphalt.

Whoever did this didn’t kill him in anger. Anger is quick, sloppy, loud. This was civic work—methodical, cold, like a demolition permit stamped and filed. A man reduced the way neighborhoods get reduced: piece by piece, until all that’s left is a lot number and a memory nobody trusts.

I lit a cigarette I didn’t want and watched the smoke curl toward the ceiling stains. In this town, everything rots eventually—fruit on the cart, promises in campaign offices, teeth behind pretty smiles. Tonight it was just his turn to show me what the city really is: a hungry machine that eats men whole and burps up clues.

results.model_response:
The sirens cut out at midnight.

That was the signal: the city had switched from *work* to *play*.

On the towers, billboards flickered from toothpaste and debt relief to the Hunt feed—thousands of windows opening at once, each tagged with a heartbeat, a name, and a betting line. Drones lifted from their charging cradles like a swarm of mechanical gnats, red lenses blinking alive. Somewhere in the upper tiers, champagne corks popped.

Down in Sector Nine, Mara ran.

Her tracker cuff blinked amber at her wrist, counting down her grace period in pitiless digital ticks. The rain had turned the alleyways to mirrors, each puddle reflecting the same thing: her own face, gaunt and slick with sweat, and the white stripe they’d painted across her jacket to make her easier to spot on camera.

“Runner 47A,” boomed a voice from the nearest loudspeaker. “Three minutes to legal pursuit. Sponsored by Halcyon Securities. Place your wagers now.”

Mara vaulted a collapsed barricade and slammed into a side street choked with rusted vending carts. Her lungs burned. Her right boot had split at the sole two blocks ago. Every step slapped water and bloodless panic onto the concrete.

Above her, a drone dipped low and projected a neon arrow onto the wall ahead: **THIS WAY TO SURVIVAL!**

She ignored it. Decoys. Always decoys.

The old subway entrance appeared where she’d hoped it would, half-buried beneath a fallen transit sign. She dropped to her knees, fingers digging into grit, and yanked the maintenance grate free. Cold air breathed up from below—stale, dark, hidden.

Then the countdown on her cuff hit zero.

Her amber light turned green.

The loudspeakers cheered.

---

On Tier Three, in a climate-controlled lounge lined with velvet and steel, Cassian Vale accepted a fresh cartridge for his rifle and smiled without warmth.

“Forty-two to one on this one,” said his assistant, eyes on the betting tablet. “Crowd thinks she’ll make the river.”

Cassian rolled his shoulders, listening to the tiny servos in his hunting suit tighten around his joints. “Crowd likes underdogs. Makes the ending sweeter.”

He stepped onto the private elevator pad, glass lowering around him like a coffin. At his temple, his HUD bloomed: thermal maps, drone feeds, Runner 47A’s pulse rising and spiking in frantic staccato.

“Remember,” the assistant said as the platform dropped, “full capture bonus if she’s conscious at retrieval.”

Cassian’s smile widened a fraction. “I always read the terms.”

---

Mara moved through the old subway tunnels by touch and memory, one hand on the wall, the other clutching the stolen signal jammer in her pocket. Somewhere ahead, if the maps from the resistance were real, there was an exit beyond the floodgates. Beyond that, maybe the dead zone. No cameras. No broadcasts. No Hunt.

She heard him before she saw him: a clean metallic click, precise as a clock hand.

Lights snapped on down the tunnel, one by one, white and blinding. Drones floated in, filling the air with a mosquito whine. Their speakers crackled with excited commentary.

“And there she is! Runner 47A entering the old Green Line. Heart rate 176. Audience spike in the north districts—welcome, viewers!”

Mara broke into a sprint. The tunnel curved. A shot cracked, sparks jumping from the rail beside her. Warning shot. Showmanship.

“Don’t,” came a voice through the drones, smooth and amplified. “I’d hate to damage my winnings.”

She hurled the jammer down the tunnel. It burst in a cone of static. Three drones dropped, stuttering into darkness. The feed glitched; the commentary died to digital shriek.

For a breathless second, silence.

Then Cassian stepped through it, visor glowing pale blue, rifle lowered but ready. He moved like he had all night and all the money in the world—which he did.

Mara swung a rusted length of pipe at his head. He caught her wrist mid-strike, twisted, and the pipe clanged away into black water. She drove her shoulder into his chest plate. He barely shifted.

“You run well,” he said, almost conversationally, as he pinned her against the tiled wall. “That’s rare.”

She spat at his visor. “Hope your viewers enjoyed the suspense.”

He tilted his head, like considering a compliment. Then he pressed a restraint band to her forearm. It cinched tight with a sharp hiss, locking her muscles into trembling stillness.

Her cuff flashed red: **CAPTURED.**

High above, every screen in the city erupted in applause.

---

Retrieval teams arrived in matte-black armor, boots splashing through tunnel water. They hooked Mara to a mag-rig and hauled her upright for the cameras. Her feet barely touched the ground.

Cassian removed his visor as the lead adjudicator approached with the ceremonial case: brushed chrome, corporate crest embossed in gold. Inside lay his prize token—a platinum key stamped with 47A’s number and tonight’s odds.

“By authority of the Civic Games Commission,” the adjudicator intoned, loud enough for every feed, “Hunter Cassian Vale claims lawful capture and associated bounty.”

Cassian took the key between two fingers. Behind him, Mara glared through wet hair, breathing hard, refusing to look down.

The adjudicator turned to her. “Runner 47A, do you concede?”

Mara said nothing.

One of the guards struck the floor beside her with a shock baton. “Answer.”

She lifted her chin and, voice ragged but clear, said, “I concede nothing.”

The audience counter on the nearest drone surged—millions tuning in for defiance, for punishment, for whatever came next.

Cassian glanced at her, then at the camera lens floating inches from his face. He held up the platinum key, letting it catch the tunnel light like a small moon.

“Send the payout,” he said.

The city roared.

The rain had turned the alleyways to mirrors, each puddle reflecting the same thing: her own face, gaunt and slick with sweat, and the white stripe they’d painted across her jacket to make her easier to spot on camera.

“Runner 47A,” boomed a voice from the nearest loudspeaker. “Three minutes to legal pursuit. Sponsored by Halcyon Securities. Place your wagers now.”

Mara vaulted a collapsed barricade and slammed into a side street choked with rusted vending carts. Her lungs burned. Her right boot had split at the sole two blocks ago. Every step slapped water and bloodless panic onto the concrete.

Above her, a drone dipped low and projected a neon arrow onto the wall ahead: THIS WAY TO SURVIVAL!

She ignored it. Decoys. Always decoys.

The old subway entrance appeared where she’d hoped it would, half-buried beneath a fallen transit sign. She dropped to her knees, fingers digging into grit, and yanked the maintenance grate free. Cold air breathed up from below—stale, dark, hidden.

Then the countdown on her cuff hit zero.

Her amber light turned green.

The loudspeakers cheered.

On Tier Three, in a climate-controlled lounge lined with velvet and steel, Cassian Vale accepted a fresh cartridge for his rifle and smiled without warmth.

“Forty-two to one on this one,” said his assistant, eyes on the betting tablet. “Crowd thinks she’ll make the river.”

Cassian rolled his shoulders, listening to the tiny servos in his hunting suit tighten around his joints. “Crowd likes underdogs. Makes the ending sweeter.”

He stepped onto the private elevator pad, glass lowering around him like a coffin. At his temple, his HUD bloomed: thermal maps, drone feeds, Runner 47A’s pulse rising and spiking in frantic staccato.

“Remember,” the assistant said as the platform dropped, “full capture bonus if she’s conscious at retrieval.”

Cassian’s smile widened a fraction. “I always read the terms.”

Mara moved through the old subway tunnels by touch and memory, one hand on the wall, the other clutching the stolen signal jammer in her pocket. Somewhere ahead, if the maps from the resistance were real, there was an exit beyond the floodgates. Beyond that, maybe the dead zone. No cameras. No broadcasts. No Hunt.

She heard him before she saw him: a clean metallic click, precise as a clock hand.

Lights snapped on down the tunnel, one by one, white and blinding. Drones floated in, filling the air with a mosquito whine. Their speakers crackled with excited commentary.

“And there she is! Runner 47A entering the old Green Line. Heart rate 176. Audience spike in the north districts—welcome, viewers!”

Mara broke into a sprint. The tunnel curved. A shot cracked, sparks jumping from the rail beside her. Warning shot. Showmanship.

“Don’t,” came a voice through the drones, smooth and amplified. “I’d hate to damage my winnings.”

She hurled the jammer down the tunnel. It burst in a cone of static. Three drones dropped, stuttering into darkness. The feed glitched; the commentary died to digital shriek.

For a breathless second, silence.

Then Cassian stepped through it, visor glowing pale blue, rifle lowered but ready. He moved like he had all night and all the money in the world—which he did.

Mara swung a rusted length of pipe at his head. He caught her wrist mid-strike, twisted, and the pipe clanged away into black water. She drove her shoulder into his chest plate. He barely shifted.

“You run well,” he said, almost conversationally, as he pinned her against the tiled wall. “That’s rare.”

She spat at his visor. “Hope your viewers enjoyed the suspense.”

He tilted his head, like considering a compliment. Then he pressed a restraint band to her forearm. It cinched tight with a sharp hiss, locking her muscles into trembling stillness.

Her cuff flashed red: CAPTURED.

High above, every screen in the city erupted in applause.

Retrieval teams arrived in matte-black armor, boots splashing through tunnel water. They hooked Mara to a mag-rig and hauled her upright for the cameras. Her feet barely touched the ground.

Cassian removed his visor as the lead adjudicator approached with the ceremonial case: brushed chrome, corporate crest embossed in gold. Inside lay his prize token—a platinum key stamped with 47A’s number and tonight’s odds.

“By authority of the Civic Games Commission,” the adjudicator intoned, loud enough for every feed, “Hunter Cassian Vale claims lawful capture and associated bounty.”

Cassian took the key between two fingers. Behind him, Mara glared through wet hair, breathing hard, refusing to look down.

The adjudicator turned to her. “Runner 47A, do you concede?”

Mara said nothing.

One of the guards struck the floor beside her with a shock baton. “Answer.”

She lifted her chin and, voice ragged but clear, said, “I concede nothing.”

The audience counter on the nearest drone surged—millions tuning in for defiance, for punishment, for whatever came next.

Cassian glanced at her, then at the camera lens floating inches from his face. He held up the platinum key, letting it catch the tunnel light like a small moon.

“Send the payout,” he said.

The city roared.

Rain had turned the trench wall into a slick, breathing thing. Mud slumped in heavy folds, swallowing boots to the ankle, then the calf, as if the earth itself wanted men back. Private Thomas Hale had stopped feeling his toes sometime before dawn. He could still feel the weight of his rifle, the stink of wet wool, cordite, and rot, and the thin shiver in his jaw that wouldn’t leave.

Then the shelling lifted.

For a few suspended seconds there was only the drip of water and the wheeze of men trying to remember how to breathe. Hale was peering over the firing step when a shadow dropped into the trench two bays down—gray coat, blackened face, helmet askew. German.

Someone shouted. Someone fired and hit dirt.

The enemy soldier lunged forward, slipping in mud, and Hale moved on instinct more than thought. His rifle caught on a sandbag and was jerked from his hands. He reached for the nearest thing: the entrenching tool hanging from his belt, a short-handled shovel with a sharpened edge from months of digging and cutting roots.

The German turned into him, close enough that Hale saw he was young, no older than twenty, with rainwater running off his eyelashes. They crashed together against the timber revetment. Hale smelled sour sweat and tobacco on his breath. The man grabbed Hale’s sleeve with both hands and drove him down. Their boots slid. Their knees hammered in the muck.

Hale swung the shovel once, clumsy. It struck the man’s shoulder with a wet thud. He yelled—not a word, just raw sound—and struck Hale across the face with something hard, maybe the butt of a pistol, maybe a fist wrapped in metal. White light burst in Hale’s skull. He tasted blood, hot and salty.

Then fear took over, simple and total.

He drove upward with the shovel edge like he was splitting frozen ground.

The blade bit into the side of the man’s neck. Not cleanly. It stuck. The soldier made a choking noise, hands flying to the wound, eyes suddenly huge with disbelief, with accusation. Hale yanked the shovel free, slipping, and struck again. This time the man folded, knees buckling, body crumpling into the trench water with a heavy splash that sounded obscenely ordinary, like a sack dropped from a cart.

Everything else came back at once—rifle cracks, shouted orders, another shell whining overhead—but it reached Hale as if through thick glass. He stared at the man he had just killed. The gray coat darkened, spreading in the mud. One hand twitched twice and went still.

Hale realized he was still raising the shovel, ready to strike a third time at a body that wasn’t moving.

“Tom! Tom!” someone was yelling at him, grabbing his webbing, shaking him.

He couldn’t answer. His arms were locked. His teeth chattered though he wasn’t cold anymore. He looked at his hands and did not recognize them: mud to the wrists, blood in the creases, knuckles split open. His stomach lurched. He turned and vomited into the trench drain, dry-heaving until his ribs cramped.

When the barrage started again, the others ducked by reflex. Hale did too, but slowly, like an old man. He crouched with his back to the wall and held the shovel across his lap like it might jump away. Every few seconds his eyes snapped to the dead soldier’s face.

The face was wrong now—slack, pale beneath the grime, mouth parted as if still trying to say something. Hale kept seeing him alive, rain on his lashes, that one instant of shared panic before the blow landed. Not an enemy then. Just a man who had also been afraid.

By evening, Hale had stopped shaking. His voice worked. He accepted tea. He even nodded when a sergeant clapped his shoulder and called him lucky.

But when night came and the trench settled into its low chorus of coughs, snores, and distant guns, he lay awake with his eyes open. Each time he blinked he felt the resistance in his hands again: the jolt of impact, the drag of metal through flesh, the terrible intimacy of it. He pressed his palms into the mud until they hurt, as if pain might prove he was still here and not trapped in that single minute forever.

At stand-to before dawn, he cleaned the shovel carefully, methodically, scraping along the edge with a bit of rag until the steel shone dull in the gray light. When he finished, he wrapped it and hooked it back on his belt.

His hands were steady.

That frightened him most.
